items.title: Henry A. "Hank" Kmen Interview, 1963-02-13
items.q: When Gottschalk came here in the 1850s, of course, he was a hometown boy

ctx.x: It seems to me that until the twenties, around in there, the professional jazz musician in New Orleans came definitely from a working class family. And he didn't, uh, maybe have all the advantages of a musical education. I don't know.

I think this fits in though, you see? Just as a, look at it this way. A great many Negroes today, Uh huh. Excel in music, just as they excel in, say, football. Because this is one of the avenues that is open to them, where they can make a mark and go a considerable distance. And this might attract a larger percentage. Let's say that among the whites, there might be a larger percentage having a good deal of native musical ability. But they have opportunities that are so good in the field of law or business or…
What about funeral music in those days? Can you infer anything about it? You come across that?
